docs.title: AI for EE Research
docs.text:
Title: AI for EE Research: From Researcher to Orchestrator

Target Audience: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research

Prerequisites:

  • Graduate standing (or equivalent research experience) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, or a related field
  • Working knowledge of at least one programming language, preferably Python
  • Basic comfort with a command line, a text editor, and Git
  • Experience writing a technical paper or report
  • No prior machine learning, prompt engineering, or agent experience required

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text:
Graduate research in electrical engineering and computer design is a pipeline of repeatable tasks: finding and reading literature, brainstorming and scoping a problem, writing analysis and simulation code, processing data, and preparing figures and manuscripts. Generative AI tools and agents can now take a substantial share of each of these tasks, but only for researchers who know how to direct them, check their output, and take responsibility for the results.

This course is a hands-on guide to that skill. Its central idea is a change in the researcher's role: from doing every task personally to orchestrating a team of agents. In the vision developed throughout the book, each researcher coordinates roughly 20 planning agents, which explore literature, decompose problems, and draft specifications, and 10 execution agents, which write code, run analyses, build simulations, and prepare figures and manuscripts. The researcher's job is to set direction, supply domain judgment, resolve conflicts between agents, and decide what is true. The researcher stays accountable for the science.

The course is practical rather than theoretical. Students learn the two building blocks that make agents reliable in a research setting: plain Markdown files that capture a project's goals, conventions, and constraints, and reusable agent skills that turn a repeatable research task into a single, testable command. Throughout, the course works from case studies of real work, including AI-generated interactive simulations (MicroSims), intelligent textbooks, and a full paper prepared for arXiv with AI agents, and it treats effective, creative, responsible, and ethical use as equal goals.

The course also teaches personal knowledge graphs: a researcher's own notes, papers, experiments, people, and projects, represented as linked entities and relationships rather than as a folder of files. A personal knowledge graph gives agents a structured, queryable memory of the researcher's work, and the course shows how to build one with an agent, query it, use it to ground a model's answers, and decide what an agent may be allowed to see.

The course also surveys the new class of always-on personal agents that arrived in 2026, because researchers will meet them in their own labs whether or not a course introduces them. These are hosted or self-hosted agents that keep their own cloud computer, sign in to tools on the user's behalf, remember context across sessions, and work while the researcher is away. As of this writing the survey covers SpaceXAI's Grok Bot, OpenAI's Dots, Meta's Muse, Anthropic's Claude Cowork, and the open-source OpenClaw and Hermes Agent. The goal is not to rank products, which change monthly, but to give researchers durable criteria for choosing and supervising any of them: where the agent runs, what it can reach, how permissions and approvals work, what it costs, and what happens to research data. The current research notes are collected in the appendix Personal Agents.

docs.title: Main Topics Covered
docs.text:
1. The research workflow and where AI helps: literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, coding, and manuscript preparation
  2. How large language models work, at the level a researcher needs: tokens, context windows, hallucination, model selection, and cost
  3. Prompting and context engineering for research tasks
  4. Markdown as a project knowledge format: project instruction files, notes, specifications, and conventions that agents read before they work
  5. Agent skills: designing, writing, testing, and sharing reusable skills for repeatable research tasks
  6. Agents and tool use: file access, shell commands, web search, subagents, hooks, and connecting to external tools and data
  7. Planning agents and execution agents: dividing work, handoffs, and coordination
  8. Orchestration: the researcher as the coordinator of 20 planning agents and 10 execution agents
  9. AI-assisted literature search, reading, and synthesis
  10. AI-assisted data analysis and scientific coding, including scripts for simulation, signal processing, and plotting
  11. AI-assisted brainstorming, problem framing, and hypothesis development
  12. AI-assisted manuscript preparation: structure, LaTeX, figures, references, and arXiv submission
  13. Interactive simulations (MicroSims) and intelligent textbooks as ways to communicate and teach research results
  14. Verification, validation, and reproducibility of AI-assisted work
  15. Responsible and ethical use: citation, disclosure, privacy, intellectual property, bias, and academic integrity
  16. Case studies of AI-assisted research and publication workflows, including the MicroSims arXiv paper and intelligent textbook projects
  17. Personal agents: always-on hosted and self-hosted agents such as Grok Bot, Dots, Muse, Claude Cowork, OpenClaw, and Hermes Agent, including their architectures, permission and approval models, multi-agent features, pricing, and data-handling trade-offs
  18. Personal knowledge graphs: representing a researcher's notes, papers, and projects as entities and relationships, building them with agents, querying them, using them as grounded agent memory, and protecting their privacy

docs.title: Topics Not Covered
docs.text:
• Training, fine-tuning, or building large language models from scratch
  • Machine learning theory, deep learning architectures, and neural network mathematics
  • AI hardware design, accelerators, and chip architecture for AI workloads
  • Vendor-specific electronic design automation (EDA) flows and tool tutorials
  • Domain-specific EE theory such as circuit analysis, device physics, or quantum electronics (the course assumes students bring this knowledge)
  • Legal advice on copyright, patent, and data-protection law
  • Comparative benchmarking and rankings of commercial AI products
  • Using AI to replace the researcher's judgment, authorship, or accountability

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: After completing this course, students will be able to:

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
Retrieving, recognizing, and recalling relevant knowledge from long-term memory.

  • Define the key terms: token, context window, prompt, agent, subagent, skill, tool call, hallucination, and orchestration
  • List the five everyday research tasks this course targets: literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, coding, and manuscript preparation
  • Recall the purpose of a project instruction file and the typical sections it contains
  • Identify the parts of an agent skill: name, description, instructions, and supporting files
  • Name common failure modes of AI output, including fabricated citations, silent errors in code, and overconfident summaries
  • State the difference between a planning agent and an execution agent
  • Name the major personal agent products (Grok Bot, Dots, Muse, Claude Cowork, OpenClaw, and Hermes Agent) and the vendor or project behind each

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
Constructing meaning from instructional messages, including oral, written, and graphic communication.

  • Explain why a language model can produce fluent but false statements
  • Describe how context window limits affect long research tasks
  • Explain why Markdown is a good format for knowledge that both humans and agents read
  • Summarize how an agent differs from a chatbot, and how tool use extends what it can do
  • Describe how an always-on personal agent differs from a session-based assistant, including where it runs, how it signs in to tools, and how it keeps memory between sessions
  • Explain how a personal knowledge graph differs from a folder of notes, and how entities, relationships, and backlinks make a researcher's knowledge queryable by an agent
  • Explain how splitting work between planning and execution agents reduces errors and cost
  • Describe the researcher's responsibilities when AI contributes to a result, including citation and disclosure

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
Carrying out or using a procedure in a given situation.

  • Write a project instruction file that gives an agent the goals, conventions, and constraints of a research project
  • Use an AI tool to run a literature search and produce an annotated reading list with verified citations
  • Prompt an agent to write, run, and debug an analysis script on a real dataset
  • Create a reusable agent skill that automates one repeatable task from their own research workflow
  • Use an agent to draft a manuscript section from notes, then revise it into their own voice
  • Generate an interactive simulation that illustrates a concept from their research
  • Build a personal knowledge graph from their own research notes and papers using an agent for entity extraction, then query it to ground an agent's answers

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
Breaking material into constituent parts and determining how the parts relate to one another and to an overall structure or purpose.

  • Decompose a research project into tasks suited to planning agents and tasks suited to execution agents
  • Compare the output of several agents on the same task and identify where and why they disagree
  • Trace an error in AI-generated code or a claim in AI-generated text back to its source
  • Distinguish tasks that benefit from AI assistance from tasks that require the researcher's direct work
  • Analyze a case study of an AI-assisted research project and map its workflow, handoffs, and review points
  • Compare personal agents on architecture, permission and approval model, multi-agent support, integrations, and cost, separating vendor claims from independently tested behavior

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
Making judgments based on criteria and standards through checking and critiquing.

  • Verify AI-generated citations, numerical results, and code against primary sources and independent tests
  • Judge whether an AI-assisted result meets the standard for reproducibility in their field
  • Assess a skill or agent workflow for reliability, cost, and risk before relying on it
  • Critique an AI-assisted manuscript for accuracy, originality, and proper attribution
  • Decide when and how to disclose AI assistance to a venue, advisor, or collaborator under ethical and institutional guidelines
  • Assess the security and data-handling risks of giving a personal agent access to research accounts, unpublished data, and licensed tools before adopting it
  • Decide which parts of a personal knowledge graph an agent may read, and assess the privacy risk of exposing unpublished results through it

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Putting elements together to form a coherent or functional whole; reorganizing elements into a new pattern or structure.

  • Design an orchestrated team of planning and execution agents for a research project, with defined roles, handoffs, and review checkpoints
  • Build a personal library of agent skills and project instruction files for their research group
  • Produce a complete, verified research artifact with agent assistance, such as a literature review, an analysis notebook, or a draft paper
  • Develop a responsible-use policy for AI in their lab or research group
  • Capstone project: plan and run an end-to-end research task with a coordinated team of agents, document the workflow, and present the verified results along with an honest account of where human judgment was required

docs.title: Appendix: Personal Agents
docs.text:
Research notes — not yet a finished chapter

This appendix holds raw research gathered on October 15, 2026. Nearly every claim is vendor-stated or comes from press coverage; we found no independent benchmarks or controlled tests of any product listed here. Prices, tiers, and features changed several times within weeks of launch, so verify against each vendor's own pages before relying on a number.

docs.title: Why this matters for EE research
docs.text: A personal agent is an AI system that does not just answer a question but carries out multi-step work on your behalf — signing in to tools, running routines, and coming back when it is done or needs a decision. For a researcher, that could mean overnight literature sweeps, rerunning an analysis when new lab data lands, or filing bug tickets against a simulation toolchain. The products below all arrived within roughly two months of each other in mid-2026, so the category is moving fast.

docs.title: Grok Bot (SpaceXAI)
docs.text: SpaceXAI announced Grok Bot on August 11, 2026, as an early-beta, cloud-based agent service. "Bot" is the product name; it is not the ordinary Grok chatbot. It appears to be the first joint product of xAI and Cursor. Sources disagree on whether SpaceX is acquiring Cursor or merging with it (MacRumors cites a $60 billion acquisition), so treat the deal terms as unsettled.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
• Persistent cloud computer. Each user gets a cloud machine with a browser, files, and a terminal. Work continues when the user's laptop is off.
  • Signs in like a human. Bots log in to websites and apps, including services that offer no API or MCP integration.
  • Teachable routines. A user shows a bot a task once; it saves the routine and later runs it on its own.
  • Multiple bots. Several bots can share one group chat, share context, and hand work to each other. A manager bot can delegate to specialist bots. AIMultiple reports up to six bots per group chat and "Team Bots" on Teams/Enterprise plans (public beta since September 28).
  • Memory. Bots keep memory across conversations and may start work "before you need to ask," per SpaceXAI.
  • Interface. Work is assigned in a chat window on desktop or iOS. The bot returns a result or asks for approval.

SpaceXAI's own example uses include updating a CRM from call transcripts, onboarding new hires and processing invoices in Gmail, and reproducing a bug, filing a ticket, and handing the fix to a debugging bot.

docs.title: Security claims and open questions
docs.text:
SpaceXAI states that Grok Bot uses Cursor SSO and authentication, privacy mode, encryption in transit and at rest, a training opt-out, and an "Auto Review" step for sensitive actions. Enterprise admins can configure data-loss prevention, certificates, proxies, and network controls.

Open questions raised by analysts:

  • Shared logins. Isolation is per user, not per bot. All of a user's bots share one computer, including its files, browser, and logins, so one compromised bot exposes the rest.
  • Undocumented details. Retention defaults, credential handling, permission granularity, audit records, which actions need approval by default, and whether memory can be viewed or edited.
  • Reliability. Nothing documents failure handling or what happens to a saved routine when a website's interface changes.
  • Cost surprises. Cursor itself warns that an hourly routine or a busy Slack trigger "can use a week of usage in a day."

docs.title: Dots (OpenAI)
docs.text:
OpenAI introduced Dots at DevDay on September 29, 2026, as a personal agent inside ChatGPT, powered by GPT-6 Astra.

  • Always-on. A dot runs in the background with its own cloud computer and browser, pursuing goals with minimal oversight.
  • App ecosystem. It can use the 4,000+ apps already connected to ChatGPT and can delegate coding to Codex.
  • Visibility. The user can open a dot's "computer" at any time to see what it is doing, and can connect a dot to their own PC.
  • Communication. A dot can message or call the user with progress, questions, or decisions. Slack and Microsoft Teams integrations were announced; text-message support is described as coming later.
  • Safety model. Passwords used for sign-in are not exposed to the underlying model. Proactive background research uses read-only app access. Dots have built-in rules for when to act versus ask, and users can write custom approval rules. OpenAI says it is working with Microsoft to bring Dots under Agent 365 security controls.
  • One dot for now. Each eligible user gets one primary dot they can name and customize. OpenAI says it expects "teams of Dots working together," but multi-dot control is not available at launch.
  • Availability. Launched for Pro and Business Premium users in "eligible markets"; reports differ on whether Business and Enterprise are included, and some exclude the EEA, Switzerland, and the UK for personal accounts.

Conflicting price reports

Engadget reports the first dot is free for Pro and Business Premium subscribers. AIMultiple lists a $100/mo starting price. We could not reconcile the two; check OpenAI's own announcement.

TechCrunch notes that much of what Dots do was already possible with Codex and similar agent harnesses — Dots package those capabilities around independent action.

docs.title: Muse (Meta)
docs.text:
Meta launched Muse on September 8, 2026, in the U.S. for users 18 and older, as a separate app that also runs inside WhatsApp. It is aimed at everyday tasks: schedules, shopping, travel, and turning long-term goals into plans.

  • Architecture. Each user's agent runs in its own cloud virtual machine.
  • Permissions. A layer called Sentinel decides whether each connected-app action and outbound request is allowed, blocked, or sent for approval. Meta says the agent never sees your actual passwords or payment details, and each purchase needs approval showing exact details.
  • Visibility. Users can watch the agent's browser as it works and review an activity log.
  • Memory. Stored as editable text files.
  • Pricing. Free tier, plus $20/mo (Power) and $100/mo (Maximum) tiers with weekly token allowances.
  • Privacy. Training on user data is on by default, with an opt-out.
  • Integrations. Centered on Meta's platforms plus email, calendar, payments, and a handful of consumer categories — narrower than the developer-oriented tools.

docs.title: Claude Cowork (Anthropic)
docs.text:
Cowork launched in January 2026 and became generally available on April 9, 2026. It lives in a tab inside Claude Desktop, where Claude reads your files, runs multi-step tasks, and uses plugins and MCP connectors.

  • Platforms. macOS first, with Windows following in February 2026. Anthropic's download page also lists Linux and ChromeOS builds.
  • Scheduled tasks. Added February 25, 2026. A March 2026 source says they require the computer to be awake and Claude Desktop open, which makes Cowork the least "always-on" of the commercial products. That may have changed since.
  • Dispatch. Lets you assign a task from your phone.
  • Pricing. No separate SKU: it is included in Claude Pro ($20/mo), Max ($100 or $200/mo), Team, and Enterprise plans. Agentic tasks reportedly burn usage allowances five to twenty times faster than ordinary chat, and the usage pool is shared with Claude chat and Claude Code.
  • Enterprise. Role-based access control, per-group spend limits, and usage analytics. One source notes Cowork activity is not yet captured in audit logs or the Compliance API.

docs.title: Open-source alternatives: OpenClaw and Hermes Agent
docs.text:
• OpenClaw is an MIT-licensed, self-hosted agent that lives in chat apps such as WhatsApp, Telegram, and Discord. You choose the model (Claude, GPT, Gemini, or a local model through Ollama). Model usage is the main cost — one estimate is $5–50/month. Reviews report reliability problems: runaway loops, malicious skills, and unattended deletions.
  • Hermes Agent (Nous Research, public since February 25, 2026) is also MIT-licensed. It runs on a laptop, server, or cloud sandbox, supports many model providers, and has a learning loop that writes its own skills. The trade-off is that you manage your own servers, secrets, and security.

Press describes Grok Bot as "a user friendly OpenClaw": the same idea, hosted and managed, in exchange for openness and control.

docs.title: Contrast: what actually differs
docs.text:
• Grok Bot's differentiator is the manager/specialist bot model. OpenAI says multi-dot control is planned but not shipped; Muse is one agent per user.
  • Grok Bot is the least transparent. Models are undisclosed, usage allowances are unpublished, and the shared-login design widens the blast radius of any one failure. Dots and Muse document their approval rules more explicitly.
  • Dots lean on the ChatGPT ecosystem — its apps, Codex, and voice calls.
  • Muse targets consumers, with the strongest purchase-approval story but the narrowest work-tool integrations.
  • Cowork is session-oriented and the most mature knowledge-work tool, but the least autonomous.
  • OpenClaw and Hermes trade convenience for control: you pick the model and own the security.

docs.title: Caveats and gaps
docs.text:
• No independent testing. AIMultiple's comparison reports no benchmarks or controlled tests of Dots, Grok Bot, or Muse; the only first-hand evidence is the author's anecdotal use of Grok Bot.
  • Moving prices. Tiers and prices changed within weeks of each launch.
  • Beta status. SpaceXAI's October 12 pages checked by Kingy.ai do not say whether Grok Bot is still in beta.
  • Source bias. Many comparison blogs host or sell one of the products they rank.
  • Unread source. The Neowin article returned HTTP 403 and was not read directly.
  • Cowork currency. The newest Cowork source we found is from August 2026.

docs.title: Questions to resolve before this becomes a chapter
docs.text:
1. Which of these agents suits an EE research workflow (long simulations, licensed EDA tools, lab data) — and which cannot reach those tools at all?
  2. What is each agent's behavior on sensitive or unpublished research data (training defaults, retention, memory)?
  3. How should a research group audit what an always-on agent did overnight?
  4. Which claims can the author verify first-hand with a hands-on trial?

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This textbook is organized into 20 chapters covering 379 concepts.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator - Introduces the research workflow, the five everyday research tasks, core generative AI vocabulary, and the central idea of the researcher as an orchestrator of agent teams.
  2. How Language Models Work - Explains tokens, context windows, prompts, training data, and hallucination so researchers understand why models produce fluent but sometimes false output.
  3. Choosing Models and Writing Clear Prompts - Covers choosing among models by size, cost, and access, adding retrieval, and writing clear, constrained prompts with examples and output formats.
  4. Context Engineering and Advanced Prompting - Develops context engineering, grounding, prompt testing, and multi-step prompting, along with defenses against prompt injection and long-document problems.
  5. Markdown Project Files and Version Control - Teaches Markdown, project instruction files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, and the Git practices that keep project knowledge organized and reliable.
  6. Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill - Builds project knowledge through notes, logs, and knowledge bases, turns a researcher's notes into a personal knowledge graph that agents can query, then introduces the parts of an agent skill.
  7. Designing, Testing, and Sharing Agent Skills - Shows how to scope, test, version, share, and maintain agent skills, ending with a template for turning a repeatable research task into a skill.
  8. Agents, Tool Use, and Subagents - Describes the agent loop, tool calls, file and shell access, sandboxing, permissions, the Model Context Protocol, and subagents that work in parallel.
  9. Supervising Agents and Defining Agent Roles - Covers autonomy, supervision, logging, failure modes, and cost control for agents, then defines the planning, execution, and reviewer roles agent teams need.
  10. Orchestrating Teams of Planning and Execution Agents - Shows how to coordinate teams of planning and execution agents through task queues, handoffs, approval gates, delegation, and scaling decisions.
  11. AI-Assisted Literature Search and Synthesis - Applies agents to search strategy, paper triage, summarization, citation verification, and evidence synthesis for rigorous literature reviews.
  12. AI-Assisted Data Analysis and Scripting - Uses AI to clean, explore, visualize, and analyze measurement data with Python scripts and notebooks while keeping errors visible.
  13. Simulation, Testing, and Reproducible Code - Covers unit tests, debugging, silent errors, simulation and HDL code, parameter sweeps, and reproducible environments for AI-written research code.
  14. Brainstorming and Problem Framing - Applies AI to framing problems, generating and ranking ideas, developing hypotheses, designing experiments, and checking novelty.
  15. AI-Assisted Manuscript Preparation - Walks through paper structure, drafting, revision, author voice, LaTeX, figures, references, peer review responses, and arXiv submission with AI assistance.
  16. MicroSims and Research Communication - Uses slide decks, interactive simulations, MicroSims, learning graphs, and intelligent textbooks to communicate and teach research results.
  17. Verification and Reproducibility - Presents verification and validation methods, including independent and cross-model checks, replication, audit trails, and tracing errors to their source.
  18. Responsible and Ethical Use of AI - Addresses citation and disclosure of AI use, privacy, intellectual property, bias, institutional and journal policy, accountability, and over-reliance.
  19. Always-On Personal Agents for Research - Surveys always-on personal agents such as Grok Bot, Dots, Muse, Claude Cowork, OpenClaw, and Hermes Agent, then shows how to compare, secure, and select them and how a personal knowledge graph serves as their memory.
  20. Case Studies and Capstone Project - Applies the whole toolkit through case studies, including the MicroSims paper and intelligent textbook project, and closes with the capstone project and adoption plan.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
Work through the chapters in order. Each chapter lists the earlier chapters it builds on, and every concept appears in exactly one chapter, after the concepts it depends on. Early chapters build the foundations of models, prompts, project files, and skills; middle chapters apply agents to the five research tasks; late chapters cover verification, ethics, always-on personal agents, and the capstone.

Note: Each chapter includes a list of concepts covered. Make sure to complete prerequisites before moving to advanced chapters.

docs.title: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
Summary

docs.title: Learning Graph for AI for EE Research
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
The 379 concepts in the AI for EE Research learning graph are organized into 17 categories. Each concept has exactly one primary category, identified by a 3-6 letter TaxonomyID that is used in learning-graph.csv and as the group key in learning-graph.json. The categories follow the course's teaching order: foundations first, then how models work, then the Markdown and skill building blocks, then agents and orchestration, then the five research tasks, and finally verification, ethics, and the capstone. The always-on personal agents and personal knowledge graph categories were added afterward and are numbered last so that existing concept IDs did not change.

No category holds more than 10% of the concepts, well under the 30% ceiling.

docs.title: FOUND — Foundations of AI-Assisted Research
docs.text: Concepts 1-20. The research workflow, the five target tasks, the core vocabulary of generative AI and agents, and the central idea of the researcher as orchestrator.

docs.title: LLM — How Language Models Work
docs.text: Concepts 21-50. Tokens, context windows, prompts and completions, training data, hallucination, model selection and cost, retrieval, and the interfaces researchers use to reach a model.

docs.title: PROMPT — Prompting and Context Engineering
docs.text: Concepts 51-80. Writing clear instructions, output formats and acceptance criteria, choosing and compressing context, grounding, prompt libraries, testing, and multi-step prompting.

docs.title: MDKB — Markdown and Project Knowledge
docs.text: Concepts 81-110. Markdown syntax, project instruction files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, notes, specifications, logs, knowledge bases, and the Git practices that keep them reliable.

docs.title: SKILL — Agent Skills
docs.text: Concepts 111-135. Designing, writing, scoping, testing, versioning, sharing, and maintaining reusable agent skills for repeatable research tasks.

docs.title: AGENT — Agents and Tool Use
docs.text: Concepts 136-170. The agent loop, tool calls, file access, shell commands, code execution, permissions, subagents, hooks, external data, autonomy, and agent failure modes.

docs.title: ORCH — Agent Teams and Orchestration
docs.text: Concepts 171-205. Planning and execution agents, roles, handoffs, task queues, review checkpoints, delegation, and the 20-planning-agent, 10-execution-agent orchestration model.

docs.title: LIT — Literature Search and Synthesis
docs.text: Concepts 206-225. Search strategy, paper triage and summarization, citation chaining, reference management, citation verification, and evidence synthesis.

docs.title: DATA — Data Analysis and Scientific Coding
docs.text: Concepts 226-255. Data cleaning, analysis scripts, plotting, testing and debugging, simulation and signal-processing code, HDL, and reproducible environments.

docs.title: BRAIN — Brainstorming and Problem Framing
docs.text: Concepts 256-265. Framing problems, generating and ranking ideas, developing hypotheses, designing experiments, and checking novelty.

docs.title: MANU — Manuscript Preparation
docs.text: Concepts 266-284. Paper structure, drafting and revision, author voice, LaTeX, figures, references, arXiv submission, peer review response, and authorship.

docs.title: COMM — MicroSims and Research Communication
docs.text: Concepts 285-296. Slide decks, MicroSims, interactive simulations, intelligent textbooks, learning graphs, and teaching from research.

docs.title: VERIF — Verification and Reproducibility
docs.text: Concepts 297-312. Verification and validation, independent and cross-model checks, result replication, sycophancy and overconfidence, audit trails, and error tracing.

docs.title: ETHIC — Responsible and Ethical Use
docs.text: Concepts 313-336. Academic integrity, citation and disclosure of AI use, privacy, intellectual property, bias, institutional and journal policy, accountability, and over-reliance.

docs.title: CASE — Case Studies and Capstone
docs.text: Concepts 337-350. The MicroSims arXiv paper, the intelligent textbook project, lessons learned, agent team design, and the capstone project.

docs.title: PERS — Always-On Personal Agents
docs.text: Concepts 351-369. Always-on, cloud-hosted and self-hosted personal agents: persistent cloud computers, delegated sign-in, taught routines, the individual products (Grok Bot, Dots, Muse, Claude Cowork, OpenClaw, and Hermes Agent), blast radius, usage metering, comparison criteria, vendor-claim verification, research-data exposure, overnight audits, and agent selection. See the appendix Personal Agents.

docs.title: PKG — Personal Knowledge Graphs
docs.text: Concepts 370-379. Knowledge graphs, entities and relationships, personal knowledge graphs built from a researcher's own notes and papers, graph schema, backlinks, entity extraction, graph querying, graph retrieval augmented generation, knowledge graph memory for agents, and the privacy of personal knowledge.

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
1. Topic count and overlap (-1). Topics 7 (planning and execution agents) and 8 (orchestration) cover closely related ground. They can stay separate for concept generation, but consider grouping the 16 topics under four or five themes for chapter planning.
  2. EE specificity in Apply (-1). The outcomes read as generally applicable to any research field. Adding two or three EE and computer-design tasks (for example generating a testbench, scripting a parameter sweep, or cleaning measurement data) would anchor the learning graph in the audience's domain.
  3. Named case studies in Analyze (-1). The case-study outcome refers to case studies generically. Naming them (for example the MicroSims arXiv paper and a specific intelligent textbook) would let the graph include concrete case-study concepts.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
Prioritized by their effect on concept generation:

  1. Add two or three EE or computer-design examples to the Apply level.
  2. Name the specific case studies once the talk content is final.
  3. Optionally add a short "Course Format" section (duration, hands-on versus lecture, expected tools). The rubric does not score it, but it helps chapter design.

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
Estimated concepts: about 220-260.

  • 16 topics at an average of 12-16 concepts each gives roughly 190-260 concepts.
  • Six Bloom's levels with 4-6 outcomes each suggest a healthy mix of vocabulary, procedural, and evaluative concepts.
  • Topics 4 and 5 (Markdown and skills) and topic 14 (verification) are the densest and are likely to produce the most concepts.
  • Likely to fall short only if the case-study chapter stays generic.

docs.text: Score is at or above 85, so the course description is ready for learning graph generation. Recommended next skill: learning-graph-generator.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small, interactive educational simulations — each one focused on a single concept. They live under docs/sims/<sim-name>/ and are embedded into chapters via iframes.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).
